827.title: Bhishma's honest answer
827.hook: the Pandavas ask their own grandsire how he can be killed, and he tells them the truth

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Krishna leapt from the chariot and ran at Bhishma on foot, a God who bends for his devotees, and Bhishma welcomed him. Your line: bhakta vatsala: god bends for his devotees. And the old man is still standing.

segments.voice: Night, and the Pandava camp is quiet in the wrong way. Another day has gone to Bhishma, the commander of the other side and the elder these brothers grew up calling grandsire. Yudhishthira can't see a way through. Then he remembers the first morning, when he walked over to Bhishma unarmed. Bhishma promised him counsel then, and told him to ask another time how he could be beaten. So the brothers set their weapons aside, and with Krishna they walk across the dark field to the enemy's tent.
screen: `ANOTHER DAY LOST TO BHISHMA.` → `A PROMISE OF COUNSEL.` → `ACROSS THE FIELD AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Bhishma doesn't reach for a sword. In Ganguli's English, he welcomes them. Yudhishthira asks it out loud: how can you be defeated? And Bhishma answers. As long as he holds his bow, no one can bring him down. But there is a warrior he will not fight. Shikhandi, Drupada's child, was born a daughter, and Bhishma has vowed never to raise a weapon against one he counts as a woman. Put Shikhandi in front, he tells them, and let Arjuna shoot from behind. Walking back, Arjuna comes apart. He remembers climbing into Bhishma's lap as a boy and calling him father, and Bhishma gently correcting him: not your father, child, your father's father. How can I kill him? It's the same grief that opens the Bhagavad Gita, where Arjuna asks how he can aim arrows at Bhishma and Drona, men he should worship. Now the teaching. In Hinduism, truth, satya, sits at the heart of dharma. Bhishma's whole life is built on keeping his word; two days ago you met the Bhishma pratigya, a vow that binds for life. Tonight his truthfulness costs him his life. But the epic won't make him simple. The same loyalty to his vow keeps him on the wrong side of this war. Dharma, the Mahabharata keeps saying, is subtle.
screen: `HOW CAN YOU BE DEFEATED?` · `SHIKHANDI IN FRONT` · `A BOY IN HIS GRANDSIRE'S LAP` · then, large: `SATYA: TRUTH IS DHARMA`

segments.voice: Sit tall and let your breath settle. Hindu students have long heard a teacher's charge from the Taittiriya Upanishad: satyam vada, dharmam chara. Speak the truth; walk in dharma. Breathing in, say satyam vada silently. Breathing out, dharmam chara. Then bring to mind one true thing you've been putting off saying, and just hold it for a moment. If you pray, offer it in your prayer. If you don't, let it be a quiet resolve.

828.title: Amba, born again
828.hook: the warrior Bhishma won't fight carries a grievance from a whole lifetime before the war: the princess Amba
828.carry: karma can follow you into another birth
828.tomorrow: two kinds of arrows hit Bhishma. can he tell them apart?

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-TWENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the Pandavas crossed the dark field, and Bhishma kept to satya, telling them the truth that would end him. Your line: satya: truth is dharma, even against yourself.
screen: `THE TRUTH THAT WOULD END HIM.` · `SATYA: TRUTH IS DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Why Shikhandi? Bhishma has held off whole armies without flinching. Why would one warrior from Drupada's house make him lower his bow? The epic's answer starts long before this war, before the Pandavas were born, at a bride-choosing in the kingdom of Kashi. Bhishma arrives there, not for himself, but for his younger half-brother, who needs a wife. He carries off the princesses of Kashi in his chariot. One of those princesses is named Amba. Today, her story.
screen: `WHY SHIKHANDI?` → `A BRIDE-CHOOSING IN KASHI.` → `A PRINCESS NAMED AMBA.`

segments.voice: Back in Hastinapura, Amba says her heart was already given to King Shalva. Bhishma lets her go to him. But Shalva won't take her back: another man carried you off, he says in effect, go to him. And Bhishma won't take her either. Long ago he swore never to marry, the vow that, the text says, earned him the name Bhishma, the one of the terrible vow. Every door is shut, and in Amba's eyes one man shut them all. Even Parashurama, Bhishma's own teacher, fights him for her and can't win. So Amba turns to austerity, and Shiva grants her wish: in another birth she will be the cause of Bhishma's death. She enters the fire, and is born again in King Drupada's house as a daughter, raised as a son, who later becomes a man, Shikhandi. And Bhishma knows all of it. When he lowers his bow before Shikhandi, he's looking at Amba. Here's the teaching under the story. Hindus believe in karma and rebirth: what we do bears fruit, and the self, the atman, isn't finished when one body ends. The Gita puts it simply: as a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves one body and takes another. A wrong done in one life doesn't vanish. And notice who did it: not a villain, but a man keeping a promise to his father and winning brides for his brother. Good intentions don't cancel karma.
screen: `EVERY DOOR SHUT` · `SHIVA'S PROMISE` · `BORN AGAIN AS SHIKHANDI` · then, large: `KARMA ACROSS BIRTHS`

segments.voice: Hindus have an old way of carrying karma: offering what you do to God. In the Gita, Krishna says whatever you do, whatever you eat or give, make it an offering to me, and many families end a puja with the words Krishnarpanam astu: may this be offered to Krishna. Bring to mind one choice you made for good reasons that still landed hard on someone. Breathe in and see the person it reached. Breathe out and, if you pray, offer it: Krishnarpanam astu. If you don't, simply wish that person well.

829.title: The bed of arrows
829.hook: two kinds of arrows reach Bhishma, and he can tell them apart
829.carry: uttarayana: even the hour of death is sacred
829.tomorrow: his head is hanging down. what pillow will he take?
829.howItsDone: Many Hindus remember Bhishma around Makar Sankranti and on Bhishma Ashtami, and the bed of arrows, in Sanskrit shara-shayya, appears in temple art, paintings and retellings of the epic.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-TWENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday we went back a lifetime, to Amba, born again as Shikhandi. Your line: karma can follow you into another birth.
screen: `BHISHMA'S FALL.` · `AMBA BECOMES SHIKHANDI.`

segments.voice: Two kinds of arrows are flying at Bhishma's chariot. Some come from Shikhandi, standing in front, exactly as Bhishma himself advised. Bhishma doesn't answer them. He keeps his bow lowered toward that one warrior, the way he said he would. And behind Shikhandi, using him as cover, Arjuna is shooting too. Bhishma has trained and fought beside these archers for a lifetime. Today, the moment he stops guessing whose arrows are reaching him.
screen: `SHIKHANDI IN FRONT.` → `BHISHMA WON'T ANSWER.` → `ARJUNA BEHIND.`

segments.voice: In Ganguli's English, Bhishma speaks as the arrows pierce him. These aren't Shikhandi's, he says, in effect. They cut too deep. These are Arjuna's. Still he doesn't turn his weapons on Shikhandi. Then he falls from his chariot. So many arrows are lodged in him that he never touches the ground. He lies on them, held above the earth, on a bed of arrows. The fighting stops. Both sides gather around the same old man. And Bhishma doesn't die. Long ago his father gave him a gift for his vow: he would die only when he chose. Hindus call it ichchha-mrityu, death at will. Lying there, he sees the sun in its southern course and decides it isn't yet time. Sages come to him as swans, sent by his mother, the river goddess Ganga, and he tells them he'll hold on until the sun turns north. Here's why that matters. Hindu tradition treats the sun's northern half of the year, uttarayana, as the bright, auspicious time, and the Bhagavad Gita names those six months among the bright paths by which those who know God depart. So Bhishma doesn't just pick a day. He picks a holy one. Hindus still keep the memory: Makar Sankranti is celebrated as the sun's turn north, and Bhishma Ashtami, a few weeks later, marks the day tradition says he let go. The teaching: in Hinduism, the hour of leaving this life isn't something to hide from. It can be faced, prepared for, and offered to God.
screen: `THESE ARE ARJUNA'S ARROWS` · `DEATH AT WILL` · `WAITING FOR THE SUN` · then, large: `UTTARAYANA`

segments.voice: Turn toward wherever the sun is right now, even through a wall. Many Hindus greet the sun each morning, palms together or pouring out a little water, with a simple line: Om suryaya namah. I bow to the sun. Breathe in and feel the light on your face, or imagine it. Breathe out and say the line once, silently or aloud. If you pray, let the greeting be your prayer. If you don't, let the light remind you that your days have a direction.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-THIRTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Bhishma fell onto a bed of arrows and chose uttarayana, the sun's turn north, for his hour. Your line: uttarayana: even the hour of death is sacred. Today, the last scene of this stretch.
screen: `THE BED OF ARROWS.` · `UTTARAYANA: A SACRED HOUR.`

segments.voice: His body is held up by arrows, but his head isn't. It hangs down, unsupported. Bhishma asks for something to rest it on. And the kings around him do the obvious thing. They run to their tents and come back with pillows, soft ones, fine ones, the best in the camp. Bhishma turns them all away. These don't belong on a bed like this one, he says, in effect. Then he looks at Arjuna. Today, what a grandson brings instead of a pillow, and the last thing Bhishma asks of the war.
screen: `HIS HEAD HANGS DOWN.` → `SOFT PILLOWS.` → `HE SENDS THEM AWAY.`

segments.voice: Bhishma asks Arjuna for a pillow fit for a hero's bed, and Arjuna understands. With tears in his eyes, the text says, he drives arrows into the ground beneath the old man's head, so it rests on them. The same grandson whose arrows brought him down. Later, when he's thirsty, Arjuna shoots an arrow into the earth, and cool water springs up for him. Then he spends his strength on one more piece of counsel, to Duryodhana. Let the war end with me, he says, in Ganguli's telling. Make peace with your cousins and let everyone go home. Duryodhana hears it and refuses. The war goes on. But this bed isn't finished. Bhishma will lie on it past the end of the war, and when the fighting is over, Krishna brings Yudhishthira here to learn. That teaching fills whole books of the epic. One is called the Shanti Parva, the Book of Peace, the peace Duryodhana turned down today. And in the book after it, Yudhishthira asks: who is the one God, the highest refuge? Bhishma answers with a hymn of a thousand names of Vishnu, the Vishnu Sahasranama. Hindus chant it in homes and temples to this day. The teaching: in Hinduism an elder's last words are treasured, and the best of them lead back to God. Bhishma lost the argument for peace. He handed down a prayer that's still being said.
screen: `A PILLOW OF ARROWS` · `LET THE WAR END WITH ME` · `THE BOOK OF PEACE` · then, large: `A THOUSAND NAMES OF VISHNU`

segments.voice: The thousand names open with one word: vishvam, the whole universe. Many teachers read it as saying God is all of it. Sit back and let your breath settle. Breathing in, think vishvam. Breathing out, let the word widen to everything around you: the room, the street, the people you love and the ones you don't. If you pray, let each breath be a name of God. If you don't, let the word simply mean: all of it, held together.

segments.voice: A teacher takes command of an army sent against his own students. Bhishma lies on the field, and the man the Kauravas choose to lead them is Drona, the master of arms who trained both sets of cousins as boys, who once tested the princes with a toy bird in a treetop and found that only Arjuna saw nothing but its head. Duryodhana honors him, and Drona, pleased, offers him a gift: ask for whatever you want. Duryodhana's answer surprises him. Not Arjuna's death. Not victory. Bring me Yudhishthira, he says. Alive.
screen: `THE TEACHER TAKES COMMAND.` → `TEACHER OF BOTH SETS OF COUSINS.` → `BRING ME YUDHISHTHIRA ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Drona is glad to hear it, at first. In Ganguli's telling, he praises Duryodhana: you don't want your cousin killed, so maybe you mean to make peace. But Duryodhana's reasons show. A captured Yudhishthira could be drawn into the dice again, and the Pandavas sent back to the forest. Same game, second round. Drona agrees, with one condition: only if Arjuna isn't beside him. So a band of Trigarta warriors swears an oath to challenge Arjuna and never come back until he's dead or they are: the samshaptakas, the sworn ones. Arjuna won't refuse a challenge, and he rides away. Now step back, because this part of the story asks something hard. Hindus hold the teacher, the guru or acharya, almost as high as God. The Taittiriya Upanishad tells a student leaving school: treat your mother as a god, your father as a god, your teacher as a god. Acharya devo bhava. That's why, on the war's first morning, Yudhishthira walked unarmed to Drona, bowed to him and asked his blessing. Drona gave it, and told him plainly that he was bound to the Kaurava side by what they had given him. So the epic holds both: the teacher is sacred, and a teacher can still stand on the wrong side. Arjuna will honor Drona and fight him. In the coming days, that empty space where Arjuna should be will matter.

segments.voice: Morning, and across the field Drona has arranged his army into a shape the Pandavas dread: the chakra, the wheel. Ring inside ring of chariots, elephants and warriors, turning to close around anyone who comes near. On the Pandava side, only a few know how to break it. Arjuna knows. Krishna knows. And Arjuna is far away on the other side of the field, answering the sworn ones' challenge, just as the plan intended. Yudhishthira looks around and finds one more person who might know: Arjuna's son, Abhimanyu.
screen: `THE WHEEL FORMATION.` → `ARJUNA IS FAR AWAY.` → `ARJUNA'S SON, ABHIMANYU.`

segments.voice: Abhimanyu is the son of Arjuna and Subhadra, Krishna's sister: young, fearless, already a fine warrior. Yudhishthira asks him to break the wheel, and his answer is honest. In Ganguli's telling, he can pierce the formation, but if trouble comes he can't come out again. Bhima promises they'll follow through his gap. So Abhimanyu drives in, breaks the ring, and he's inside, fighting brilliantly. But behind him Jayadratha, king of Sindhu, rides into the breach. The text says he once won a gift from Shiva: for one day he could hold back all the Pandavas except Arjuna. This is that day. The wheel closes, with one young man inside. Now the part so many Hindu families add. In the popular retelling, Abhimanyu learned the way in before he was born: Arjuna explained the wheel to Subhadra while she carried him, and she fell asleep before the way out. That isn't in the epic's own passage here. But it rests on something Hindu tradition really holds: a child is listening before birth. The Bhagavata Purana says Prahlada learned devotion to Vishnu inside his mother's womb, hearing the sage Narada teach her. Hindu tradition also keeps some life-rites, the samskaras, before birth, and many Hindu families today sing bhajans and play mantras for a baby on the way. Abhimanyu's half-heard lesson is the sad side of the same belief: what a child hears early, they carry into the wheel.
screen: `I KNOW THE WAY IN, NOT OUT` · `JAYADRATHA HOLDS THE GAP` · `HEARD IN THE WOMB` · then, large: `A CHILD IS LISTENING`

segments.voice: Many Hindus begin and end their prayers with one sound, Om. Breathe in deeply. On the way out, let a low Om hum through your chest, and feel it in your bones before you hear it. Do it three times. Then bring to mind a child you love, or the child you once were, and wish them good things to hear. If you pray, let the Om be your prayer. If you don't, let it simply be a sound you give to someone small.

segments.voice: He has no bow anymore. His horses are down, his charioteer is gone, his sword is broken. And Abhimanyu bends down and picks up a chariot wheel, lifts it like a weapon, and keeps fighting. That picture is where the day ends up. It starts with him tearing through the Kaurava ranks inside the formation, so fiercely that, in Ganguli's telling, even Drona speaks admiringly of his skill. Today, the end of Abhimanyu, and the promise his father makes that night.
screen: `NO BOW, NO HORSES, NO SWORD.` → `HE LIFTS A CHARIOT WHEEL.` → `EVEN DRONA ADMIRES HIM.`

segments.voice: Drona admires the boy, and still commands: take his bow first. Karna cuts it from behind. Others bring down his horses and his charioteer. Then the great warriors of the Kaurava side close around one young man together. Abhimanyu fights on with sword and shield until they break, then with the chariot wheel, then with a mace. At last the son of Duhshasana strikes him down. Here's why Hindus remember this as one of the war's darkest hours. Before the first arrow flew, both sides agreed on rules for a righteous war, a dharma yuddha. Fight your equal, one to one. Never strike someone whose weapon is broken, who has no armor, who is already fighting another. Abhimanyu died against nearly every one of them. The teaching: dharma doesn't switch off in a war. Even in the worst place, there's a right way and a wrong way, and the epic keeps the account. Days later, when Karna's own chariot wheel sinks in the mud and he pleads for a fair fight, Krishna asks him where that dharma was when many surrounded the boy. That evening, Arjuna rides back and senses something is wrong before anyone speaks. When he learns his son is dead, and that Jayadratha held the gap, his grief becomes a vow. Before tomorrow's sun sets, he'll kill Jayadratha, and if he fails, he'll enter the fire himself.

segments.voice: If you'd like, rest one hand over your heart and bring to mind someone young you care about: a child, a niece, a student, a younger friend. Many Hindus close a prayer with three words: om shanti, shanti, shanti. Peace, peace, peace. Breathe in and picture them clearly. Breathe out and say it, once for them, once for the world around them, once for your own heart. If someone you loved died too young, let them be here too, gently. If you don't pray, let the words simply be a wish.
